newsitem.title: USA: Jones case adds to US political sex scandal lore.
newsitem.headline: Jones case adds to US political sex scandal lore.

text.p: The latest turn in the sexual harassment case against President Bill Clinton adds to the crop of Washington sex scandals for which the American public appears to have limitless appetite.

The case of Paula Jones, a former Arkansas state employee who alleged that then-Governor Clinton exposed himself and asked her for oral sex, had been dormant for months but resurfaced on Tuesday when the Supreme Court ruled that the case need not wait until Clinton leaves the White House.
If it gets to trial, it could set a legal precedent but would hardly be the first time politics and sex have been linked in the public mind.

Last year, for example, Clinton campaign adviser Dick Morris stole the president's thunder during the Democratic National Convention when it was revealed that he had carried on a long-running affair with a prostitute and had a child with another woman. The affair was front-page news for weeks.
Clinton himself weathered campaign questions in 1992 about his then-troubled marriage and his own alleged relationship with lounge singer Gennifer Flowers.

Before that, the presidency of George Bush was touched by a whiff of scandal in the case of Bush's Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas, who was alleged to have sexually harassed fellow attorney Anita Hill when both worked at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Senate hearings into the matter ended with Thomas being confirmed, but not until "sexual harassment" became a household phrase. The issue dominated the media and sent reported cases of sexual harassment soaring.

Gary Hart's 1988 White House hopes foundered after he dared reporters to follow him and they discovered that he had entertained model Donna Rice. The married senator from Colorado pulled out of the race, then got back in, but never came close to winning the Democratic nomination.

Other Washington politicians' peccadilloes are part of the city's lore: Representative Wilbur Mills' inamorata, stripper Fannie Foxe, gamboling in the Tidal Basin after a lovers' spat; Marilyn Monroe's breathy, public "Happy Birthday" serenade to President John F. Kennedy; President Franklin Roosevelt's reported dalliance with a secretary.

It is axiomatic that sex sells newspapers, but Washington Post media critic Howard Kurtz suggested in a column that there might be another reason for the persistent popularity of Washington sex scandals: "A prurient interest in issues that are rarely debated openly in American society unless they are 'legitimized' by being packaged as news stories."
Sexual scandal hit the U.S. presidency in its infancy, with accusations against President Thomas Jefferson that he had fathered children with a black slave.
But sometimes just the aura of Washington seems to pull sexual scandals into its orbit and into the headlines.

The recent matter of Air Force Lt. Kelly Flinn, the female bomber pilot who narrowly evaded court-martial for, among other offences, adultery, became Washington news because of its ramifications at the Pentagon, which was already smarting from other sex-related cases.

Even as the Supreme Court released its decision in the Jones case, one of television's leading sportscasters, Marv Albert, was being arraigned across the Potomac River in Arlington, Virginia, on charges of sexual assault and battery on a woman in a hotel room in February. Albert's attorney said he planned to plead not guilty.
